Synthesis of defect-rich metal-free carbon from coconut shell for catalyzing 
oxygen evolution reaction

ABSTRACT
Biomass-derived carbon materials represent stable, cost-effective and environmentally friendly electrocatalyst for 
oxygen evolution reaction (OER) and hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). In this work, a self-supporting coconut 
shell carbon (SCC) catalyst featuring a three-dimensional (3D) hierarchical porous structure was reported by in 
situ ammonia etching. The SCC-1100-NH
3 
exhibited outstanding OER performance, achieving a current density 
of 10 mA cm
� 2 
at an overpotential of 294 mV and a potential of 1.52 V vs RHE. The unique structural config -
uration also offered the catalyst excellent durability with stable operation for at least 98 h. It was believed that 
the hierarchical porous structure enhances electrical conductivity and the formation of vacancy-coupled 
pentagon defects which act as active sites. This work provides a new strategy for designing defect-rich metal- 
free biomass-derived carbon electrodes.
1. Introduction
Oxygen evolution reaction (OER) is a critical process in renewable 
energy technologies, yet its practical application is hindered by intrin -
sically slow kinetics involving a four-electron transfer, which leads to 
high overpotentials ( η > 200 mV) [ 1 – 3 ]. This inefficiency remains a key 
obstacle in devices such as electrolysers, regenerative fuel cells and 
metal-air batteries. Although noble metal oxides (e.g., IrO
2 
and RuO
2
) 
represent the state-of-the-art OER catalysts due to their high activity and 
stability [ 4 ], their high cost and limited availability impede widespread 
use [ 2 , 5 ]. Moreover, under harsh oxidizing conditions, these catalysts 
often suffer from dissolution or surface reconstruction, further under -
mining their long-term stability. These challenges have motivated the 
search for cost-effective and durable alternatives. Metal-free carbon- 
based materials such as biomass-derived carbons, graphene and carbon 
nanotubes [ 6 ], have gained increasing attentions because of low cost, 
tunable electronic properties, high stability, and the use of earth- 
abundant precursors.
The OER on metal-free carbon catalysts operates through a mecha -
nism fundamentally different from that of conventional metal-based 
oxides [ 7 ]. Instead of relying on metal d-orbitals, the catalytic activity 
stems from modifications to the electronic structure of the carbon 
framework. Heteroatom doping with elements such as nitrogen, boron, 
phosphorus and sulfur, enables precise redistribution of charge within 
the carbon matrix. For instance, pyridinic nitrogen provides lone elec -
tron pairs, while graphitic nitrogen enhances conjugation, and both ef -
fects promote charge polarization to form highly active sites that may 
act synergistically to improve electrocatalytic performance [ 8 – 12 ]. 
Notably, engineered carbon defects can exhibit higher catalytic efficacy 
than even pyridinic-N sites in certain doped graphitic carbons [ 13 ], 
establishing defects as emerging active centers in carbon-based elec -
trocatalysis. Structural imperfections such as vacancies, edges and to -
pological defects break the continuity of the sp
2
‑ carbon network. This 
exposes carbon atoms with mixed sp
2
/sp
3 
hybridization, altering local 
electron density and creating regions of enhanced charge that favor the 
adsorption of OH
�
and stabilize key intermediates like *OOH, thereby 
lowering the Gibbs free energy barrier [ 14 – 16 ]. Dangling bonds at 
defect sites also strengthen interactions with hydroxy species, promot -
ing O
–
O bond formation [ 14 , 17 ]. Therefore, designing carbon archi -
tectures with a high density of defects is an effective strategy for 
improving metal-free OER catalysts. Biomass-derived carbon materials 
have attracted considerable interest in this regard due to their innate 
heteroatom doping and abundant structural defects. During pyrolysis, 
cross-linking reactions produce polyaromatic compounds with limited 
long-range order. At elevated temperatures, however, highly crystalline 
graphitic microdomains can develop [ 18 ]. During thermal treatment, 
structural defects such as dislocations, grain boundaries, vacancies and 
micropores could be formed through thermal stress and etching by

hydrogen radicals ( ⋅ H) that result from intense decomposition, atomic 
rearrangement, and gas release [ 19 – 21 ].
Powder-based catalysts continue to dominate electrocatalysis owing 
to mature fabrication protocols and broad applicability. However, their 
implementation necessitates polymeric binders and conductive addi -
tives for electrode assembly. These inactive components, while essential 
for structural integrity and electrical connectivity, introduce detri -
mental effects: they physically mask active sites, impeding reactant ac -
cess; promote interfacial degradation during prolonged electrochemical 
cycling; and compromise mechanical robustness, collectively under -
mining long-term electrode durability [ 22 , 23 ]. These limitations have 
accelerated the development of self-supporting electrocatalysts. Such 
systems eliminate auxiliary additives, leveraging intrinsic architectures 
that provide efficient mass transport pathways and maximized active 
site exposure. Concurrently, their monolithic design confers superior 
mechanical stability and enhanced electrochemical resilience, offering a 
promising alternative to conventional powder-based configurations. 
Nevertheless, achieving optimal performance requires navigating the 
critical trade-off between activity and robustness. The central challenge 
lies in engineering self-supporting catalysts with idealized three- 
dimensional (3D) porous architectures that simultaneously deliver 
high catalytic efficiency and operational stability.
Leveraging its inherent fibrous layered structure, which carbonizes 
into a naturally porous framework rich in interconnected channels, co -
conut shell serves as an advantageous precursor material. Subsequent 
etching of this structure can yield highly conductive carbon scaffolds 
featuring 3D interconnected lamellar channels abundant in defects 
[ 24 , 25 ], providing numerous active sites for OER while maintaining 
excellent mechanical strength and structural stability [ 26 , 27 ]. There -
fore, to fabricate porous and defect-rich self-supporting coconut shell 
carbon (SCC) plates from discarded coconut shell, this study employed 
ammonia (NH
3
) etching during the pyrolysis process. At elevated tem -
peratures, NH
3 
decomposes into reactive species (NH
2
, NH, and H) [ 28 ]. 
Atomic hydrogen (H) etches the carbon skeleton, generating micropores 
and structural defects [ 21 ]. Concurrently, NH
2 
radicals provide active 
nitrogen atoms that either substitute carbon atoms within the lattice or 
occupy defect sites, forming nitrogen-doped configurations such as 
pyridinic N and graphitic N [ 29 ]. Furthermore, nitrogen-containing 
groups can displace oxygen-containing functional groups in the pre -
cursor, optimizing the surface chemistry. Crucially, this combined 
etching and nitrogen doping disrupts the carbon layer regularity, 
inducing lattice distortion, thereby effectively introducing structural 
defects and creating a wealth of active sites [ 30 – 33 ]. Among the syn -
thesized materials, the SCC samples prepared under NH
3 
atmosphere at 
1100 
◦
C (denoted as SCC-1100-NH
3
) exhibited the optimal structural 
and electrochemical properties. Notably, the etched coconut shell car -
bon retained high mechanical stability. Abundant active sites, structural 
defects, nitrogen doping, and robust mechanical integrity collectively 
contribute to the SCC-1100-NH
3 
material with exceptional OER activity 
and stability in alkaline media.
2. Experimental section
2.1. Chemical reagents
Absolute ethanol (CH

Macklin. Coconut shells were sourced from a local market in Haikou, 
Hainan Province, China. All chemicals were used as received without 
further purification. Ultra-pure water (18.2 M Ω⋅ cm) was used

2.2. Material synthesis
SCC plates were synthesized via direct pyrolysis of discarded coconut 
shells. The coconut shells were fragmented into small pieces, washed 5 
times with a mixed solution of deionized water and ethanol (in a 1:1 
ratio) to remove surface impurities, and subsequently dried to constant 
weight in a forced-air oven at 130 
◦
C for 12 h. Pyrolysis was performed 
in an atmospheric tube furnace under a continuous flow of ammonia gas 
(50 sccm). The samples were heated to a series of target temperatures 
(900, 1000, 1100, and 1200 
◦
C) at a rate of 5 
◦
C min
� 1

held at each respective temperature for 4 h. The resulting products were 
correspondingly labeled as SCC-900-NH

a Quantachrome Autosorb iQ-MP instrument. Specific surface areas 
were calculated using the Brunauer – Emmett – Teller (BET) method, and

analysis. Microstructural and morphological analysis was performed 
using field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) on a 
Thermo Scientific Helios 5 CX instrument operated at 5 kV and trans -
mission electron microscopy (TEM) and high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) 
on an FEI Talos F200X instrument operated at 200 kV. Elemental 
mapping and composition analysis were conducted via energy- 
dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) coupled to the TEM. Raman spec -
troscopy was carried out at room temperature using a Thermo Scientific 
DXRxi spectrometer (USA) equipped with a 532 nm excitation laser. 
Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy, also referred to as 
electron spin resonance (ESR), was employed to characterize defect 
density using a Bruker EMX Plus spectrometer operating at X-band fre -
quency (~9.85 GHz).
2.4. Working electrode fabrication and electrochemical measurements
Fabrication of working electrodes involved mechanically polishing 
the synthesized SCC samples to dimensions of 0.5 cm (length) × 0.5 cm 
(width) × 0.05 cm (thickness). These polished samples underwent 
sequential ultrasonication in deionized water and absolute ethanol to 
eliminate surface impurities and oxides, followed by vacuum drying. All 
electrochemical measurements were performed at ambient temperature 
using a Instruments CH660E electrochemical workstation within a 
standard three-electrode configuration. The three-electrode system 
comprised the fabricated SCC sample as the working electrode, a 
graphite rod counter electrode, and a Hg/HgO reference electrode (1 M 
KOH). The electrolyte was 1 mol L
� 1 
KOH solution, continuously satu -
rated with N
2 
gas to ensure an oxygen-free environment. Prior to testing, 
electrode surfaces were electrochemically activated through 50 
consecutive cyclic voltammetry (CV) cycles at a scan rate of 50 mV s
� 1

2.5. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations
This study employs first-principles calculations based on DFT using 
the projector augmented wave (PAW) method, as implemented in the 
Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP) [ 34 ]. The exchan -
ge – correlation interactions are treated with the Per -
dew – Burke – Ernzerhof (PBE) form of the generalized gradient 
approximation (GGA) [ 35 , 36 ]. A (3 × 3 × 1) Γ -centered k-point grid is 
used for Brillouin zone sampling to ensure an adequate description of 
the electronic structure and total energy. A plane-wave cut-off energy of 
550 eV is applied to achieve good basis set convergence. For structural 
optimization, all configurations underwent full relaxation of both 
atomic positions and lattice parameters using the conjugate gradient 
method to minimize the total energy and internal stresses. The geometry 
optimization was considered converged when the energy difference 
between successive self-consistent field (SCF) iterations fell below 1.0 ×
10
� 6 
eV and the maximum force on any atom was less than 1.0 × 10
� 2 
eV/Å. To better describe long-range dispersion interactions in molecular 
and crystalline systems, Van der Waals corrections were incorporated in 
all calculations [ 37 ].
